title: Theological vocabulary: λόγος, φύσις, οὐσία, χάρις, πίστις, δικαιοσύνη

objectives.can: Give the range of senses of λόγος, φύσις, οὐσία, ὑπόστασις, πρόσωπον, χάρις, πίστις and δικαιοσύνη in the New Testament and in fourth-century use, without reading later definitions back into earlier texts.

explanation.summary: Eight Greek nouns carry much of the weight of Christian argument in the fourth century: λόγος, φύσις, οὐσία, ὑπόστασις, πρόσωπον, χάρις, πίστις and δικαιοσύνη. Every one of them was an ordinary Greek word first, and the New Testament uses them in ordinary senses. This lesson gives each word's range of senses, shows real New Testament verses, and describes how fourth-century writers used it, without reading later definitions back into earlier texts.

sections.heading: Before you read: how to approach these words
body: A word has a range of senses, and the context chooses among them. The questions to ask of any verse are: who is writing, when, and what does the sentence need? A later definition, fixed by a council or a school, is evidence about the later period. It is not evidence about what an earlier writer meant.

The fourth-century examples in this lesson come from Athanasius, On the Incarnation. Its analysis in this library is automatic and unchecked, and some of its labels are wrong; the glosses shown beside the words are dictionary glosses chosen by the program, not a decision about the sense in a given sentence. The lesson's own claims about those words rest on the sentences quoted.

sections.heading: The eight words at a glance
body: The table gives, for each headword, its ordinary sense, some New Testament verses where it occurs, and one or two uses in Athanasius. It describes usage and does not decide any doctrinal question.

sections.heading: οὐσία, ὑπόστασις, πρόσωπον: ordinary words before technical ones
body: In the New Testament οὐσία occurs only in the parable of the two sons: the younger asks τὸ ἐπιβάλλον μέρος τῆς οὐσίας (Luke 15:12), and the father then divides τὸν βίον, 'the living'. The word means property. Nothing in these verses is philosophical. In Athanasius the word is used in its other ordinary Greek sense, 'being' or 'substance': the Word 'is outside the universe κατ' οὐσίαν' (17.1), the body shares the same οὐσία as all human bodies (20.4). Fourth-century church debates built technical words on οὐσία; the precise sense was argued for decades, and some contemporaries objected that the word was not found in Scripture. The right way to read a sentence is to ask which sense that author needs.

ὑπόστασις has a similar history. In 2 Corinthians 9:4 it is confidence ('this boasting-confidence'); in Hebrews 11:1 πίστις is ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις, and translators have given 'assurance', 'substance' and 'reality'. In Hebrews 1:3 the Son is χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ, 'the exact imprint of his ὑπόστασις'. These verses show a range of senses, and Hebrews gives no definition. In the later fourth century some writers treated ὑπόστασις and οὐσία as near-equivalents while others separated them; usage was not fixed.

πρόσωπον means 'face' first: ἐν προσώπῳ Χριστοῦ (2 Corinthians 4:6), πρόσωπον πρὸς πρόσωπον (1 Corinthians 13:12). From 'face' come 'presence' and 'person'. In Galatians 2:6 it is idiomatic: πρόσωπον θεὸς ἀνθρώπου οὐ λαμβάνει, 'God does not accept a person's outward standing'. In Athanasius 3.5, ἐκ προσώπου τοῦ Θεοῦ means that Scripture speaks as if in God's own role. In the later fourth century Greek theologians used πρόσωπον for 'person' in talking about the Father, the Son and the Spirit.

sections.heading: λόγος and φύσις
body: λόγος is among the widest words in Greek. In 1 Corinthians 1:18 it is the 'message' of the cross; in Luke 16:2 it is an 'account' that the manager must give (compare Matthew 12:36); in John 1:1 it is the Word who was πρὸς τὸν θεόν. In Athanasius 3.3, λόγος is a title of the Son (τοῦ ἰδίου Λόγου) and, a few lines later, a plain 'principle': κατὰ τὸν τῆς ἰδίας γενέσεως λόγον. The edition's capital letters show an editor's reading, not something the manuscripts decide.

φύσις is what something is by its own constitution or birth. In Romans 2:14 Gentiles who φύσει do what the law requires, 'by nature' or 'naturally'. In Galatians 4:8 the gods who φύσει μὴ οὖσι θεοῖς are not gods 'by nature'. 2 Peter 1:4 speaks of θείας κοινωνοὶ φύσεως. Athanasius uses it for what a thing is of itself: the Word is bodiless τῇ φύσει (1.3), and human beings are perishable κατὰ φύσιν (5.1). The technical debates about 'natures' belong largely to later centuries.

sections.heading: χάρις, πίστις, δικαιοσύνη
body: χάρις can be 'favour' or 'gift' (Ephesians 2:8; James 4:6), 'thanks' (2 Corinthians 9:15, χάρις τῷ θεῷ) and 'credit' (Luke 6:32, ποία ὑμῖν χάρις ἐστίν;). Which sense is meant depends on the sentence. In Athanasius 5.1, τῇ τοῦ Λόγου χάριτι is 'by the favour (gift) of the Word'.

πίστις is 'trust', 'belief' and 'faithfulness'. In Hebrews 11:1 it is described as ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις; in Acts 6:7 ὑπήκουον τῇ πίστει uses it of the belief itself, 'the faith'. In Athanasius 3.1 ἡ κατὰ Χριστὸν πίστις is the faith 'according to Christ'. Scholars discuss the exact reach of the word in some of Paul's phrases, and this lesson does not settle those questions.

δικαιοσύνη is 'justice' in the sense of right dealing, and 'righteousness' in the sense of right conduct or standing. In Matthew 5:6 people hunger and thirst for it; in Romans 1:17 there is a δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ, and its meaning (God's own righteousness, or the righteous standing God gives) is discussed by scholars; in James 2:23 something is 'counted' for it. The English words 'justice' and 'righteousness' translate the same Greek word.

misunderstandings: Do not read the later technical senses of οὐσία, ὑπόστασις and πρόσωπον into Luke 15:12, 2 Corinthians 4:6, 2 Corinthians 9:4 or Hebrews 11:1. In those verses they are ordinary words.
A word's dictionary gloss is a starting point, not a verdict. The program's gloss for οὐσία is 'property', which suits Luke 15:12 and not Athanasius 17.1.
χάρις is not always 'grace' in a theological sense: in Luke 6:32 it means 'credit' and in 2 Corinthians 9:15 'thanks'.
An editor's capital letter in Λόγος is a reading, not a fact of the manuscript. Read the sentence first.

The multiple-choice questions on the headwords use the dictionary's first gloss as the right answer (for example 'justice' for δικαιοσύνη). The other senses in the table are equally part of the word's range.

deeper.heading: Why the New Testament uses these words in ordinary ways
body: The New Testament authors wrote in the ordinary Greek of their time and used words their readers already knew. Later writers had to decide how much weight to put on a few such words in a long argument, and different writers did so differently. A good reader keeps two questions apart: what the word means in this sentence, and what use later writers made of it.

examples.analysis: Three of the eight words in one verse. Λόγου is a genitive: 'of the Word'. χάριτι, dative, appears twice: 'by the favour (gift) of the Word', and again later in the verse. φύσιν, accusative after κατά, in the phrase κατὰ φύσιν: 'by nature'. The verse says that human beings are perishable by nature, and that by the favour of sharing in the Word they would have escaped that, had they stayed good.

reading.reference: Athanasius of Alexandria, On the Incarnation of the Word (De Incarnatione Verbi) 20.4 – Athanasius of Alexandria, On the Incarnation of the Word (De Incarnatione Verbi) 20.6
reading.why: Three sections in which οὐσία, φύσις and λόγος work together in a fourth-century argument. Read them with the lesson's rule in mind: ask which sense the author needs, and do not read a later definition into his words. The analysis of this text is automatic.
